senses.gloss: Ordinary and dull, with nothing to make it interesting.
examples: He spends his days on *mundane* tasks like filing and copying.
After the trip, going back to work felt painfully *mundane*.
Even the most *mundane* details matter in a police report.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the municipal pool*

senses.gloss: Belonging to the government of a city or town.
examples: The *municipal* pool opens in June.
She works for the *municipal* water department.
*Municipal* elections are held every two years.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the murdered man*

senses.gloss: Killed deliberately and unlawfully.
examples: Police identified the *murdered* man on Tuesday.
A stone wall lists the names of the *murdered* children.
The *murdered* journalist had written about corruption.

senses.gloss: Ready to kill, or full of the wish to kill.
examples: He gave me a *murderous* look and walked out.
The dictator's *murderous* regime lasted thirty years.

senses.gloss: Extremely hard or unpleasant to get through.
examples: The training schedule that spring was *murderous*.
We sat through *murderous* traffic for two hours.

senses.gloss: Dark and dirty, so that you cannot see through it.
examples: We couldn't see the bottom through the *murky* water.
The pond gets *murkier* after a heavy rain.

senses.gloss: Unclear and probably hiding something dishonest.
examples: His account of that night stayed *murky*.
The company has a *murky* history of lawsuits.

senses.gloss: Having big, stiff muscles from too much weight training, so that moving is awkward.
examples: A *muscle-bound* bouncer stood at the door.
He's so *muscle-bound* he can barely scratch his own back.
The part called for a *muscle-bound* action hero.

senses.gloss: Having large, well-developed muscles.
examples: Her arms are lean and *muscular*.
He has a *muscular* build from years of rowing.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the muscles of the body.
examples: *Muscular* pain can last for days after a hard workout.
She was diagnosed with *muscular* dystrophy as a child.

senses.gloss: Soft and wet, with no firmness left.
examples: The bananas went *mushy* in my backpack.
Cook the rice less — it came out *mushier* than last time.

senses.gloss: Sentimental in a way that is a little embarrassing.
examples: He gets *mushy* after two glasses of wine.
I skipped the *mushy* parts of the movie.

senses.gloss: Having a heavy, sweet, animal-like smell.
examples: The room had a warm, *musky* smell.
She wears a *musky* perfume in the winter.
The second candle is *muskier* than the first.

senses.gloss: Smelling damp and stale, the way a closed-up room does.
examples: The basement smells *musty* after the rain.
He pulled a *musty* old coat out of the closet.
The back room is even *mustier* than the attic.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a mutant gene*
contrast: Also a noun: *the mutants in the comic*. As an adjective it goes only before the noun.

senses.gloss: Changed by a mutation; carrying an altered gene.
examples: The lab isolated a *mutant* strain of the virus.
*Mutant* genes can be passed to the next generation.
The show is full of *mutant* superheroes.

contrast: Calling a person *mute* is dated and can offend; say *nonverbal* or *unable to speak*. *Mute* is also a verb — *mute the TV* means turn the sound off.

senses.gloss: Saying nothing, especially when you could speak.
examples: She stood *mute* while he shouted at the clerk.
He gave a *mute* nod of agreement.
The whole room went *mute* when she said it.

senses.gloss: Made quieter or softer in sound.
examples: We heard the *muted* sound of traffic through the glass.
He spoke in a *muted* voice so the baby wouldn't wake.

senses.gloss: Soft and not bright, of a color.
examples: The living room is done in *muted* grays and browns.
She prefers *muted* colors to bright ones.

senses.gloss: Held back, of a reaction or a feeling.
examples: The announcement got a *muted* response from investors.
Their celebration was *muted* by the news from home.

senses.gloss: Badly damaged, with parts cut off or torn away.
examples: Rangers found the *mutilated* body of a deer near the trail.
Vandals left the statue *mutilated* and covered in paint.
The library won't lend out *mutilated* copies.

senses.gloss: Refusing to obey the people in charge; ready to rebel.
examples: The crew grew *mutinous* after weeks without pay.
She shot him a *mutinous* look and kept typing.
The manager faced a *mutinous* staff on Monday morning.

position: both — usually before a noun; predicative in *The feeling is mutual*
contrast: *A mutual friend* is a friend the two of you share. A Russian speaker may reach for *common friend*, but *common* in English suggests *ordinary*.

senses.gloss: Felt or done by each of two people toward the other.
examples: They parted by *mutual* agreement.
The respect between them was *mutual*.

senses.gloss: Shared by two or more people.
examples: We were introduced by a *mutual* friend.
The two countries have a *mutual* interest in trade.

senses.gloss: Such that if one of two things is true or chosen, the other cannot be.
examples: The two options are not *mutually exclusive* — you can do both.
Being careful and being fast aren't *mutually exclusive*.
He treats fun and hard work as *mutually exclusive* categories.

senses.gloss: Thinking only about the short term, with no view of what comes later.
examples: The policy is *myopic* — it ignores what happens after the next election.
Cutting research is a *myopic* way to save money.

senses.gloss: Able to see near things clearly but not distant ones.
examples: Most *myopic* children need glasses by middle school.
He's been *myopic* since he was eight.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *myriad problems*
contrast: Also a noun: *a myriad of choices*. As an adjective it takes no *of*: *myriad choices*.

senses.gloss: Very many; too many to count.
examples: The city faces *myriad* problems at once.
There are *myriad* ways to cook an egg.
She listed the *myriad* reasons the plan would fail.

senses.gloss: Strange and hard to explain or understand.
examples: A *mysterious* package showed up on the porch.
Her illness has a *mysterious* cause that no test has found.

senses.gloss: Keeping things secret, so that others cannot guess what you mean.
examples: He was *mysterious* about where the money came from.
She gave me a *mysterious* smile and changed the subject.

senses.gloss: Having to do with direct spiritual experience of God or the divine.
examples: He writes about the *mystical* traditions of medieval Spain.
She had a *mystical* experience during the retreat.

senses.gloss: Strange and full of awe, as if beyond ordinary explanation.
examples: There's something *mystical* about the light in that valley.
The old house has a *mystical* pull on him.

contrast: *-ed* for the person who feels it, *-ing* for the thing that causes it: *I was mystified by the mystifying instructions*.

senses.gloss: Completely puzzled by something.
examples: I was *mystified* by the bill from the clinic.
Doctors were *mystified* when her fever broke on its own.
He gave me a *mystified* look, so I explained it again.

contrast: *Mystifying* is the thing; *mystified* is the person: *the mystifying rules left us mystified*.

senses.gloss: Hard to understand or explain, in a way that leaves people puzzled.
examples: The instructions that came with the shelf are *mystifying*.
She has a *mystifying* habit of answering questions with questions.
The ending of the movie was *mystifying* to everyone in the theater.

senses.gloss: Coming from myths and old stories.
examples: The griffin is a *mythical* creature, half eagle and half lion.
He collects stories about *mythical* beasts.

senses.gloss: Talked about but not real.
examples: That *mythical* raise never showed up.
Everyone keeps chasing the *mythical* perfect job.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *mythological figures*

senses.gloss: Belonging to the myths of a people, or to the study of them.
examples: The museum has a room of *mythological* figures in marble.
Her name comes from a *mythological* goddess.
He teaches a course on *mythological* themes in film.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a nagging doubt*

senses.gloss: Not serious but never going away, of a pain or a worry.
examples: I had a *nagging* feeling I'd left the stove on.
A *nagging* pain in his knee kept him up half the night.

senses.gloss: Always complaining and asking you to do things.
examples: He complained about his *nagging* boss the whole drive home.
Her *nagging* questions finally wore me down.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a nail-biting finish*

senses.gloss: So tense and exciting that you cannot sit still.
examples: The game came down to a *nail-biting* final minute.
It was a *nail-biting* wait for the test results.
They won in the most *nail-biting* finish of the season.

contrast: The noun is *naivety* or *naiveté*, not *naiveness*. *Naive* is mildly critical — it says someone has too little experience, not that they are simply natural.

senses.gloss: Too ready to believe people, from lack of experience.
examples: It was *naive* of me to think he'd pay me back.
She asked a few *naive* questions about how the company made money.
He's more *naive* than stupid.

contrast: Two syllables — the *-ed* is always /ɪd/, like *wicked* and *rugged*, never /neɪkt/.

senses.gloss: Wearing no clothes.
examples: The kids ran *naked* through the sprinkler.
He answered the door half *naked*.

senses.gloss: Bare, without the covering something usually has.
examples: A *naked* bulb hung over the kitchen table.
By November the branches were *naked*.

senses.gloss: Plain and not hidden, of a feeling or a fact.
examples: It was *naked* greed, plain and simple.
You can't see the comet with the *naked* eye.

senses.gloss: Having no name, or not named on purpose.
examples: A *nameless* donor paid for the new roof.
The report quotes a *nameless* official at the agency.

senses.gloss: Too vague to put a name to, of a feeling.
examples: A *nameless* fear kept him awake until dawn.
She felt a *nameless* sadness all that week.

senses.gloss: Belonging to Napoleon or to the years he ruled France.
examples: He teaches a seminar on the *Napoleonic* wars.
The museum owns a *Napoleonic* uniform.

senses.gloss: Grand and domineering, the way Napoleon is imagined to have been.
examples: The new director came in with *Napoleonic* ambitions.
He runs the department with *Napoleonic* confidence.

form: from *Narcissus*, who fell in love with his own reflection

senses.gloss: Obsessed with yourself and with how you look to others.
examples: His posts got so *narcissistic* that I stopped following him.
She was diagnosed with *narcissistic* personality disorder.
The whole speech was a *narcissistic* performance.

contrast: Also a noun, usually plural: *the narcotics squad*.

senses.gloss: Of a drug that dulls pain and brings sleep.
examples: The patient was given a *narcotic* painkiller after surgery.
*Narcotic* drugs are tightly controlled in every state.

senses.gloss: Making you sleepy or dull, like such a drug.
examples: The professor's voice had a *narcotic* effect on the class.
There's something *narcotic* about a long afternoon by the lake.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *narrative poetry*
contrast: Far more common as a noun (*the official narrative*). The adjective goes only before a noun.

senses.gloss: Telling a story; having to do with how a story is told.
examples: The class spends a month on *narrative* poetry.
The film has a simple *narrative* structure.
Her *narrative* voice changes from chapter to chapter.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to consider ideas or people different from what you are used to.
examples: It's *narrow-minded* to judge a book by its cover.
He grew up in a small, *narrow-minded* town.
The older he gets, the more *narrow-minded* he sounds.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the nose.
examples: The doctor prescribed a *nasal* spray.
*Nasal* congestion is usually the first symptom.

senses.gloss: Sounding as if the air is coming through the nose, of a voice.
examples: He has a flat, *nasal* voice that carries across the room.
Her accent gets more *nasal* when she's tired.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a nascent industry*

senses.gloss: Just coming into existence and starting to grow.
examples: The country's *nascent* film industry needs money and time.
A *nascent* friendship grew out of those weekly meetings.
The report warns about a *nascent* housing bubble.

senses.gloss: Very unpleasant to taste, smell or be out in.
examples: The medicine leaves a *nasty* taste in your mouth.
We drove home in *nasty* weather.

senses.gloss: Unkind and deliberately hurtful.
examples: She said something *nasty* and walked off.
He gets *nastier* the longer the meeting goes.

senses.gloss: Serious and likely to cause harm, of an injury or a problem.
examples: He took a *nasty* fall on the ice.
That's a *nasty* cut — you should get it looked at.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a national holiday*
contrast: Also a noun: *a foreign national* is a citizen of another country.

senses.gloss: Covering the whole country rather than one part of it.
examples: Thanksgiving is a *national* holiday.
The story made the *national* news by Tuesday.

senses.gloss: Belonging to a nation as a people.
examples: The flag is a symbol of *national* identity.
The team plays in the *national* colors.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a nationalist party*
contrast: *Nationalist* is the plain label for a party or movement; *nationalistic* adds disapproval. *Nationalist* is also a noun.

senses.gloss: Supporting the independence or the interests of one's own nation.
examples: A *nationalist* party won the election in March.
He gave a *nationalist* speech about borders and trade.
The movement had *nationalist* roots going back a century.

contrast: *Nationalistic* almost always disapproves; *nationalist* is the neutral label: *a nationalist party* vs *a nationalistic rant*.

senses.gloss: Showing too much pride in your own nation, often against others.
examples: The rally turned *nationalistic* and ugly.
His columns have grown more *nationalistic* over the years.
*Nationalistic* slogans covered the walls of the stadium.

contrast: Also an adverb: *The store ships nationwide*. Before a noun the stress moves forward: *a NATIONwide recall*.

senses.gloss: Happening or existing in every part of a country.
examples: The chain announced a *nationwide* recall.
There is a *nationwide* shortage of nurses.
Their coverage is *nationwide*.

contrast: *A native* as a noun for a local person now sounds colonial; say *a local*. For indigenous peoples, *Native* is capitalized: *Native American*.

senses.gloss: That you were born with or born into.
examples: Her *native* language is Portuguese.
He moved back to his *native* Ohio after college.

senses.gloss: Growing or living naturally in a place rather than brought there.
examples: The sugar maple is *native* to eastern North America.
*Native* grasses need far less water than a lawn.

ru: индейский, относящийся к коренным народам США
contrast: Also a noun. *Indian* for these peoples is dated in American English; many people prefer *Native American*, *Native*, or the name of the nation (*Navajo*, *Lakota*).

senses.gloss: Belonging to the indigenous peoples of the United States.
senses.ru: индейский, принадлежащий к коренным народам Америки
examples: The museum has a large *Native American* art collection.
She is *Native American* on her mother's side.
Several *Native American* languages are taught at the university.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a native-born citizen*

senses.gloss: Born in the country where you live, rather than having moved there.
examples: Only a *native-born* citizen can become president.
The city's *native-born* population is shrinking every year.
He's a *native-born* New Yorker who's never left the block.

takes: in sense 2, *for* + noun with a *to*-infinitive, or a *that*-clause: *It's natural for kids to test the rules*; *It's natural that you'd worry*

senses.gloss: Existing in nature, not made or added by people.
examples: The park protects the last *natural* wetland in the county.
We use only *natural* ingredients in the soap.

senses.gloss: Normal and to be expected.
examples: It's *natural* to be nervous before a test.
His reaction was perfectly *natural* under the circumstances.

senses.gloss: Born with an ability rather than having to learn it.
examples: She's a *natural* athlete.
He has a *natural* ear for languages.

senses.gloss: Showing people and things exactly as they are, in art or writing.
examples: The novel's *naturalistic* dialogue sounds like a recording.
He paints in a *naturalistic* style.
The lighting is *naturalistic* rather than theatrical.

senses.gloss: Having become a citizen of a country you were not born in.
examples: She became a *naturalized* citizen last spring.
The rule applies to *naturalized* Americans as well.

senses.gloss: Settled and growing wild in a place it was brought to, of a plant or animal.
examples: The shrub is now *naturalized* all along the coast.
*Naturalized* daffodils come back every spring on their own.

senses.gloss: Behaving badly, of a child or a pet.
examples: The dog has been *naughty* all morning.
He was the *naughtiest* kid in the class.

senses.gloss: Mildly indecent, in a joking way.
examples: She told a *naughty* joke at dinner.
The card had a *naughty* picture on the front.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *I felt nauseated*
contrast: *Nauseated* is how you feel; *nauseating* is what causes it. In everyday American speech many people say *nauseous* instead of *nauseated*.

senses.gloss: Feeling as if you are about to vomit.
examples: I felt *nauseated* for the whole flight.
She was *nauseated* by the smell of gasoline.
He gets *nauseated* on winding roads.

contrast: *Nauseating* is the cause, *nauseated* the feeling: *the nauseating smell left us nauseated*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel like vomiting.
examples: The smell in the back of the fridge was *nauseating*.
He described the wound in *nauseating* detail.

senses.gloss: Disgusting because of how someone behaves.
examples: Their *nauseating* self-congratulation went on for an hour.
It's *nauseating* to watch him take credit for her work.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *I feel nauseous*
contrast: In American English *nauseous* normally means *feeling sick*. Careful writers keep *nauseated* for the feeling and *nauseous* for the cause, but almost nobody says *I feel nauseated* in conversation.

senses.gloss: Feeling sick to your stomach.
examples: I felt *nauseous* after the second slice of cake.
She gets *nauseous* in the back seat.
He woke up dizzy and *nauseous*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a nautical mile*

senses.gloss: Having to do with ships, sailors and the sea.
examples: The bar is decorated in a *nautical* theme.
A *nautical* mile is longer than a mile on land.
He uses *nautical* terms for everything on the boat.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a naval officer*
contrast: *Naval* (of the navy) and *navel* (the belly button) sound exactly the same.

senses.gloss: Belonging to a navy.
examples: The *naval* base employs five thousand people.
He's a retired *naval* officer.
The two countries held a joint *naval* exercise.

senses.gloss: Deep and wide enough for boats to travel on.
examples: The river is *navigable* as far as the falls.
They dredge the channel every spring to keep it *navigable*.

senses.gloss: Easy to find your way through or around.
examples: The new site is far more *navigable* than the old one.
After the plow came through, the road was *navigable* again.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *navigational equipment*

senses.gloss: Used for finding the way, or having to do with doing so.
examples: The plane lost its *navigational* equipment in the storm.
A *navigational* error put them fifty miles off course.
Sailors once used the stars as a *navigational* aid.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *Nazi propaganda*
contrast: Always capitalized, and also a noun. Used loosely for anyone rigid about rules (*a grammar Nazi*), which many people find offensive.

senses.gloss: Belonging to Hitler's party in Germany or to its ideas.
examples: The film is about the *Nazi* occupation of Paris.
*Nazi* propaganda posters fill one wall of the archive.
He studies *Nazi* economic policy in the 1930s.

contrast: Also a noun. Capitalized for the prehistoric humans; often written with a small *n* in the insulting sense.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the extinct human species that lived in Ice Age Europe.
examples: *Neanderthal* remains were found in the cave in 1908.
Modern humans carry a little *Neanderthal* DNA.

senses.gloss: Crude and badly out of date in attitudes.
examples: His views on women are frankly *Neanderthal*.
The office had a *Neanderthal* culture until she took over.

contrast: Also an adverb: *They live nearby*. Before a noun the stress moves forward: *a NEARby store*.

senses.gloss: A short distance away.
examples: We ate at a *nearby* diner.
A *nearby* school was opened as a shelter.
The store is *nearby*, so we walked.

contrast: British English says *short-sighted*. For the figurative sense (bad planning), American English uses *shortsighted* or *myopic*, not *nearsighted*.

senses.gloss: Able to see close things clearly but not distant ones.
examples: I've been *nearsighted* since third grade.
A *nearsighted* driver shouldn't be on the road at night.
She's more *nearsighted* in her left eye than her right.

senses.gloss: Tidy, with everything in its place.
examples: Her desk is always *neat*.
Keep your handwriting *neater* than that.

senses.gloss: Very good or clever — informal, and common in American speech.
examples: That's a *neat* trick.
We saw a really *neat* old car at the show.

senses.gloss: Served with no ice and nothing added, of a strong drink.
examples: He drinks his whiskey *neat*.
Two bourbons, *neat*, please.

senses.gloss: Vague, with no clear shape or definition.
examples: His plans for next year are still pretty *nebulous*.
The job came with a *nebulous* title and no description.
The deadline grew more *nebulous* with every meeting.

position: predicative only — after a verb; before a noun it takes hyphens: *a neck-and-neck race*
form: compound — from horse racing, where two horses' necks are level

senses.gloss: Exactly level, with neither side ahead in a race or contest.
senses.ru: идущие вровень, вровень друг с другом
examples: The two candidates are *neck and neck* in the polls.
At the halfway mark the leaders were *neck and neck*.
With ten minutes left the game was still *neck and neck*.

position: both — before a noun, or right after it: *the funds needed*

senses.gloss: That someone requires; necessary for a purpose.
examples: The clinic finally got the *needed* equipment.
She made a much-*needed* change to the schedule.
Bring whatever supplies are *needed* for the trip.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *needless delay*; plus the set phrase *needless to say*

senses.gloss: Not necessary, and usually annoying or harmful as well.
examples: The new rule creates *needless* paperwork.
*Needless* to say, nobody had read the manual.
We lost an hour to a *needless* detour.

senses.gloss: Wicked and probably criminal — often said half in fun.
examples: The company was accused of *nefarious* accounting.
He assumed there was some *nefarious* reason for the delay.
Nothing *nefarious* — she just forgot to call.

senses.gloss: Bad or harmful in its effect.
examples: The layoffs had a *negative* effect on morale.
Too much screen time is *negative* for sleep.

senses.gloss: Saying no, or seeing only the bad side.
examples: She got a *negative* response from every publisher.
Don't be so *negative* — it might actually work.

senses.gloss: Showing that a substance or condition is not present, of a test.
examples: Her test came back *negative*.
Two *negative* results in a row meant he could go back to work.

senses.gloss: Less than zero, or carrying the electric charge of an electron.
examples: A *negative* number goes to the left of zero on the line.
The *negative* terminal is marked with a minus sign.

contrast: *Neglected* is the one left without care; *neglectful* is the one who fails to give it.

senses.gloss: Not given the care or attention it needs.
examples: The house looked *neglected*, with weeds up to the porch.
He writes about a *neglected* corner of American history.
The older kids felt *neglected* after the baby came.

contrast: *Neglectful* describes the person who fails to care; *neglected* describes the person or thing left uncared for.

senses.gloss: Failing to look after someone or something you are responsible for.
examples: The court found the parents *neglectful*.
He was *neglectful* of his own health for years.
A *neglectful* landlord let the building fall apart.

contrast: *Negligent* is the legal word — a negligent driver can be sued. *Negligible* means too small to matter. Don't mix them up.

senses.gloss: Careless about a duty, especially in a way the law can punish.
examples: The jury found the hospital *negligent*.
He was *negligent* in reporting the leak.
*Negligent* driving caused the crash.

contrast: *Negligible* = too small to matter. *Negligent* = careless. The two look alike but say opposite kinds of thing.

senses.gloss: So small that it can safely be ignored.
examples: The difference in price is *negligible*.
Sales in the first month were *negligible*.
The risk is small but not *negligible*.

senses.gloss: Open to discussion and able to be changed.
examples: The salary is *negotiable*.
The deadline is not *negotiable*.

senses.gloss: Possible to get through or across.
examples: The pass is *negotiable* only in summer.
The trail is barely *negotiable* in a regular car.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a neighboring town*
contrast: British spelling is *neighbouring*; American writing drops the *u*.

senses.gloss: Next to, or very near, the place being talked about.
examples: Smoke drifted in from the *neighboring* state.
We heard shouting from the *neighboring* apartment.
Two *neighboring* counties share the same water supply.

form: -ly from *neighbor* — an adjective, not an adverb
contrast: The *-ly* here builds an adjective, so there is no adverb *neighborlily*; say *in a neighborly way*. British spelling is *neighbourly*.

senses.gloss: Friendly and helpful the way a good neighbor is.
examples: It was *neighborly* of him to shovel our walk.
They gave us a *neighborly* wave from the porch.
The whole town has a *neighborly* feel.

senses.gloss: In a later style that copies ancient Greek or Roman models.
examples: The courthouse is a *neoclassical* building with tall columns.
She teaches *neoclassical* architecture.
*Neoclassical* economics still dominates the textbooks.

senses.gloss: Favoring free markets, deregulation and a smaller role for the state.
examples: The reforms were *neoliberal* in every respect.
She's writing a book about *neoliberal* trade policy.
Critics call the whole plan *neoliberal*.

senses.gloss: Of the late Stone Age, when people began to farm.
examples: The site holds a *Neolithic* burial mound.
*Neolithic* farmers cleared this whole valley.
The tools are *Neolithic*, not Bronze Age.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the neonatal unit*

senses.gloss: Having to do with babies in their first weeks of life.
examples: The baby spent a month in the *neonatal* unit.
She's a *neonatal* nurse at the county hospital.
*Neonatal* care has improved enormously since the 1970s.

contrast: Also a noun with no plural *-s*: *one Nepalese*, *two Nepalese*. *Nepali* is also used, and is the name of the language.

senses.gloss: From Nepal, or having to do with Nepal.
examples: We ate at a *Nepalese* restaurant downtown.
The *Nepalese* guides carried most of the gear.
Her husband is *Nepalese*.

form: compound — noun + participle: *nerve* + *racking* (from *rack*, the torture frame)
contrast: *Nerve-racking* is the older spelling and *nerve-wracking* is now just as common. Both are accepted in American writing, and they sound the same.

senses.gloss: Making you very anxious and tense.
examples: The wait for the results was *nerve-racking*.
Driving in that fog was the most *nerve-racking* hour of my life.
She has a *nerve-racking* habit of checking her phone mid-sentence.

form: compound — a respelling of *nerve-racking*, with *wrack* for *rack*
contrast: A variant of *nerve-racking*. Both spellings are standard in American English and sound identical; editors differ on which they prefer.

senses.gloss: Making you very anxious and tense.
examples: Public speaking is *nerve-wracking* for most people.
It was a *nerve-wracking* drive down the mountain.
The last ten minutes of the game were *nerve-wracking*.

contrast: In American English *nervy* means bold or cheeky. In British English it means *nervous* — nearly the opposite feeling.

senses.gloss: Boldly rude, or daring enough to risk it.
examples: That was a *nervy* thing to ask your boss.
She made a *nervy* call on fourth down.
He gets *nervier* every year.

position: predicative only — after a verb, or right after the noun: *a cabin nestled in the pines*

senses.gloss: Settled snugly in a sheltered spot.
examples: The village is *nestled* in a valley between two ridges.
A small chapel sits *nestled* among the trees.
The town is *nestled* right up against the border.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *net income*
contrast: Also a noun (*a fishing net*) and a verb. On a label, *net weight* is the contents without the package; *gross weight* includes it.

senses.gloss: Left after everything has been taken out or added up.
examples: The company reported a *net* loss of two million dollars.
Her *net* pay is a lot smaller than she expected.
The *net* result of all that work was nothing.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *neural pathways*

senses.gloss: Having to do with nerves or with the networks of the brain.
examples: The drug affects *neural* pathways in the brain.
They trained a *neural* network on old photographs.
*Neural* activity spikes during dreaming sleep.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a neurological exam*

senses.gloss: Relating to the nervous system or to its diseases.
examples: She was referred for a *neurological* exam.
The symptoms point to a *neurological* problem.
He runs a *neurological* research lab in Boston.

contrast: Also a noun: *he's a bit of a neurotic*. In everyday talk it just means fussy and anxious, not a medical diagnosis.

senses.gloss: Anxious and obsessive about something, out of all proportion.
examples: She's *neurotic* about germs.
He gets *neurotic* whenever the numbers dip.
There's a *neurotic* edge to his humor.

senses.gloss: Made unable to breed by an operation, of an animal.
examples: All the cats at the shelter are *neutered* before adoption.
A *neutered* dog is usually calmer around other males.

senses.gloss: Left powerless or without any real effect.
examples: Amendments left the bill *neutered*.
The committee was *neutered* by the budget cut.

senses.gloss: Not taking either side in a fight or an argument.
examples: Switzerland stayed *neutral* during the war.
Try to keep your tone *neutral* when you answer.

senses.gloss: Plain and soft, of a color.
examples: The walls are painted a *neutral* beige.
She buys *neutral* colors so everything matches.

senses.gloss: Neither acid nor alkaline; neither positive nor negative in charge.
examples: Distilled water is chemically *neutral*.
Connect the white wire to the *neutral* terminal.

senses.gloss: Seeming to go on forever.
examples: Laundry is a *never-ending* chore.
The road work outside felt *never-ending*.
She tells a *never-ending* story about her commute.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a never-say-die attitude*
form: compound — a whole phrase used as one adjective

senses.gloss: Refusing to give up, however bad things look.
examples: The team has a *never-say-die* attitude.
Her *never-say-die* spirit got them through the winter.
He's a *never-say-die* competitor.

takes: *to* + noun, in sense 3: *new to the job*
contrast: In American English *new* is /nuː/, not the British /njuː/. The same goes for *news*, *newt* and *nude*.

senses.gloss: Recently made, bought or built.
examples: They bought a *new* car in the spring.
This is the *newest* model on the lot.

senses.gloss: Not known, seen or tried before.
examples: The doctor wants to try a *new* approach.
Is there anything *new* in the report?

senses.gloss: Not yet used to something, of a person.
examples: I'm *new* to this city.
She's *new* on the job and still learning the system.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a newborn baby*
contrast: Also a noun: *the newborn slept all afternoon*.

senses.gloss: Only just born.
examples: The hospital has a separate wing for *newborn* babies.
A *newborn* calf was standing within the hour.
*Newborn* skin often peels in the first week.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *newfangled gadgets*

senses.gloss: Newly invented — said with suspicion or with a joke.
examples: Grandpa won't touch any of these *newfangled* phones.
She calls the dishwasher a *newfangled* contraption.
The shop refuses to carry *newfangled* electric models.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *newfound confidence*

senses.gloss: Recently gained or discovered.
examples: She's enjoying her *newfound* freedom.
His *newfound* fame lasted about a month.
They spent their *newfound* wealth on travel.

senses.gloss: Interesting or important enough to be reported as news.
examples: A school board meeting is rarely *newsworthy*.
The editor didn't think the story was *newsworthy* enough.
The arrest of a mayor is always *newsworthy*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *Newtonian mechanics*

senses.gloss: Based on Isaac Newton's laws of motion and gravity.
examples: *Newtonian* mechanics works fine at everyday speeds.
The problem is a standard *Newtonian* one.
He compares the *Newtonian* and the Einsteinian view of gravity.

contrast: Also a noun: *a Nicaraguan*. Always capitalized, like every nationality word in English.

senses.gloss: From Nicaragua, or having to do with Nicaragua.
examples: We stopped for *Nicaraguan* coffee on the way back.
The *Nicaraguan* team won on penalties.
Her grandparents are *Nicaraguan*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a nickel-and-dime operation*
form: compound — from the five-cent and ten-cent coins
contrast: Also a verb: *to nickel-and-dime someone* is to wear them down with small charges.

senses.gloss: Small-time and cheap; involving only trivial amounts of money.
examples: It's a *nickel-and-dime* operation run out of a garage.
I'm tired of their *nickel-and-dime* fees.
He made a living on *nickel-and-dime* repair jobs.

senses.gloss: Clever, neat and useful — informal and friendly.
examples: That's a *nifty* little tool.
She has a *nifty* trick for peeling garlic.
The second design is even *niftier* than the first.
